title: Plant nitrogen uptake preference and drivers in natural ecosystems at the global scale

text: Nitrogen (N) is the primary nutrient element limiting the growth and productivity of terrestrial plants (Mason et al., 2022). Plant preference for different soil N forms is one of the most critical strategies for acquiring soil N resources because it can mitigate N competition among plants, maintain plant growth, and contribute to ecosystem carbon (C) sequestration (McKane et al., 2002). However, the relative importance of different soil N for plants is poorly understood. Between soil ammonium +–N) and nitrate N (NO3 –N), which have been conN (NH4 sidered the main sources of N for plants, plants may prefer NH4  uptake due to its lower energy cost and faster uptake to NO3 assimilation (County et al., 2015; Moreau et al., 2019). However, + nutrition often induces a growth-limiting stress known as ammonium syndrome, which may offset the energy-saving + uptake over NO3  (Britto & Kronadvantage of NH4 zucker, 2013). Accordingly, some plant species, such as Ericaceae + uptake (Pearson & or spruce, have been found to prefer NH4 Stewart, 1993; Britto & Kronzucker, 2013), whereas, many fast-growing annual grasses and some pioneer woody plants have  uptake (Pearson & Stewart, 1993; Yi been found to prefer NO3  is more mobile than NH4 +; thereet al., 2023). text: These physiological costs and physical limitations constrain plant strategies in opposite directions, leading to considerable uncertainty regarding the relative importance of soil NH4 uptake for different plant species. In addition to NH4 , plants have recently been shown to directly assimilate soil organic N (N€asholm et al., 2009; Inselsbacher & Wanek, 2021). For instance, using 15N labelled model amino acid, previous studies have shown direct organic N uptake by a variety of plant species in arctic (Nordin et al., 2004), boreal (Persson & N€asholm, 2008; N€asholm et al., 2009), alpine (Miller & Bowman, 2003; Xu et al., 2006) and temperate ecosystems (Rains & Bledsoe, 2007). However, our knowledge of the global +, patterns of plant N uptake preferences for three N forms (NH4 , and organic N) remains limited. The limited understanding of plant N uptake preference may be partly due to the complex interactions between plant N acquisition and multiple factors (Moreau et al., 2019). Plant N acquisition strategies depend on various biotic and abiotic factors, such as plant functional types (Andersen et al., 2017; Hill et al., 2019), soil properties (Nordin et al., 2004; Zhang et al., 2016), and climatic conditions (Hill et al., 2011; Boczulak et al., 2014). Plant functional types represent the key functional strategies of plants in relation to their environment and provide important insights into plant ecological responses and adaptations to highly variable habitats (Gillison, 2013).
title: Plant nitrogen uptake preference and drivers in natural ecosystems at the global scale

text: Although research on plant N uptake preference strategies has been conducted for various plant species and terrestrial ecosystems (Harrison et al., 2008; Britto & Kronzucker, 2013; Liu et al., 2017), general patterns of the N uptake preference of terrestrial plants at the species level remain unclear. Soil N availability is considered a key factor inﬂuencing plant N uptake preferences, as it provides N resources from the soil to plants (Zhang et al., 2021). It is plausible that dominant plant species have evolved unique N uptake strategies to maximize their N acquisition in different climate zones, with different soil N form availability (Mason et al., 2022). In particular, in environments with severely limited soil N, such as alpine and boreal regions, there are notable differences in plant N uptake prefer-  or organic N) to ences for different soil N forms (NH4 mitigate strong competition for N (McKane et al., 2002). However, this is not always the case. In fact, plant N uptake preferences for different soil N forms in natural ecosystems often vary between study sites regardless of N-rich (Liu et al., 2017; Gurmesa et al., 2019) or N-limited conditions (Liu et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021). Therefore, plant N uptake may be signiﬁcantly inﬂuenced by factors other than soil N availability. For instance, changes in temperature directly affect plant N acquisition (Warren, 2009; Boczulak et al., 2014; Hu et al., 2024) due to temperature-dependent active transport of soil N at the root–soil interface (Bassirirad, 2000). Temperature can also indirectly affect plant N preference by inﬂuencing microbial activity and N cycling rates (Dawes et al., 2017; Lie et al., 2020), which, in turn, can alter the availability of different soil N forms and competition for soil N between plants and microbes (Kuzyakov & Xu, 2013). However, few studies have investigated the effects of temperature on plant N preference.
title: Plant nitrogen uptake preference and drivers in natural ecosystems at the global scale

text: Soil water content is another important factor affecting plant N absorption. Previous theoretical and experimental studies have demonstrated that root N uptake is constrained by the rate of N transport toward the root surface (Oyewole et al., 2016; McMurtrie & N€asholm, 2018). A high rate of transport toward the root surface enhances root N uptake by reducing the opportunity for soil microbes to intercept dissolved N and steepening the N concentration gradient in the rhizosphere adjacent to the root surface (McMurtrie & N€asholm, 2018; Henriksson et al., 2021).  is more mobile than NH4 + in the soil solution, However, as NO3 soil water content may differently inﬂuence plant N preference. Thus, multiple drivers of plant N uptake under different conditions should be identiﬁed to gain a better understanding of the relative importance of different forms of N to plants. Along a 3000 km transect spanning temperate and alpine grasslands with 18 species, a recent study found that, among multiple factors, soil N availability controls the uptake of different forms of N by plants (Liu et al., 2024). However, on the global scale, with highly variable climatic conditions and species types, the factors driving plant N uptake preference remain unclear. In this study, we compiled a global dataset of 101 publications on the N uptake strategies of different plant species in natural terrestrial ecosystems. text: Data collection and calculation Peer-reviewed journal articles reporting the application of 15N tracer methods to investigate plant N uptake strategies were identiﬁed by entering the following keywords in Google Scholar, the ISI Web of Knowledge, and the China Knowledge Resource Integrated Database: ‘nitrogen uptake’, ‘nitrogen preference’, ‘nitrogen strategy’, ‘nitrogen dynamics’, ‘plant nitrogen’, ‘soil nitrogen’, ‘ammonium’, ‘nitrate’, ‘organic nitrogen’, ‘15N labeling’, ‘stable nitrogen isotope’, and ‘microbial competition’. The reference lists of relevant articles were referred to in retrieving more pertinent articles. To increase data comparability, the following criteria were applied to select appropriate observations from the initial set of articles retrieved: (1) studies containing 15N uptake rates and/or the relative contribution of N forms to plant N nutrients by 15N labelling method were selected, and other methods (such as 15N natural abundance and concentration dilution) to explore plant N uptake strategies were excluded; (2) only the data from experiments with short isotopic exposure times were included to avoid transformations between 15NH4 , and studies that used the 15N tracer method to and 15NO3 explore long-term plant N retention, such as that of Templer et al. (2012), were excluded; (3) analyses restricted to species in natural plant communities in unfertilized soils were selected; (4) studies focusing on species-level N uptake but not on community-level N uptake were included; (5) as glycine (the smallest of amino acid, comprising 29% of the pool of amino-N) is a putative organic N source for plants, data using other organic N forms to represent organic N uptake were excluded from the database to make results comparable; and (6) for studies wherein uptake rates or the relative contribution of uptake rates were not directly available, we ﬁrst calculated the uptake rates by dividing the 15N uptake pools by the 15N labelling time and root biomass.

Of the 101 publications, 67 included all three N forms simultaneously. As our aim was to explore plant N 974 , and organic N were considered preference when NH4 simultaneously, we extracted 1008 observations from the 67 publications to estimate the relative contributions of the three N forms to plant N uptake. Study sites were located from 3°58 0 S to 68.63°00 0 N, covering a wide range of mean annual precipitation (MAP) (110–4600 mm yr1) and mean annual temperature (MAT) (9.6–26.6°C); the distribution of data points is shown in Fig. S1. Furthermore, as absorbing roots are mostly distributed in the topsoil, we focused on root N uptake strategies in the topsoil. The data on N uptake in the 0–10-cm soil layer accounted for more than 80% of the total dataset. Both ﬁeld and pot studies were included to estimate the global average of plant N preference because the relative contributions of all three N forms did not differ signiﬁcantly between the two experimental approaches (Fig. S2). However, only ﬁeld studies were included in the analysis of plant N preference across climatic conditions and their relationships with the environment because the plants included in the pot studies were grown in a controlled environment and, thus, did not reﬂect the inﬂuence of the local climate (Liang et al., 2023). Site-speciﬁc details, such as geographical location (latitude and longitude) and climatic factors (MAT and MAP), were also extracted. If local climate data were not reported in the original paper, MAT and MAP were obtained from the WorldClim dataset (http://www.world clim.org/). Ecosystem type, climate zone, and plant type were collected from the articles referred to in this study.

text: The ecosystems were categorized as forests, grasslands, or tundra. Wetlands and heathlands were classiﬁed as ‘others’ because of several observations of these ecosystems. The climate zones were classiﬁed into (sub)tropical, temperate, boreal, alpine, and Arctic zones, as described in a previous study (Hou et al., 2020). According to plant functional types, plants were categorized into nonwoody, shrub, conifer, broadleaf-deciduous, and broadleaf-evergreen species (Verheijen et al., 2015). In addition, an array of soil variables was recorded, including soil physicochemical properties (bulk density, water content, and pH) and soil nutrients (organic C content, total N content, C : N ratio, + content, NO3  content, and NH4 ++NO3 ) ratio). Unreported soil properties were extracted from SOILGRIDS250M 2.0 (https://soilgrids.org) using location information, as in another study (Wang et al., 2022). Statistical analysis One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) and post hoc analyses were performed to compare plant uptake rates and relative contributions among the three soil N forms. Differences in the N form contributions among ecosystem types, climate zones, and plant types were also analyzed using one-way ANOVA. Like in several previous studies (Wang et al., 2021; Yao et al., 2024), we used a linear mixed-effect model to evaluate the bivariate relationships of plant N uptake preference with variables deﬁned as climate, soil nutrient, and soil physicochemical properties. The following equation was used: Y = b0 + b1 9 X + p + e, where Y is the plant N uptake preference variable; X is the independent variable; b0 is the intercept; b1 is the ﬁxed coefﬁcient; p is the random 14698137, 2025, 3, Downloaded from https://nph.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nph.70030, Wiley Online Library on [15/09/2026].

The linear mixed-effect model was performed by the maximum likelihood estimation using the LME4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015). To assess the robustness of the relationships between plant N uptake preference and driving variables and clarify the relative importance of variables, a model selection analysis, based on the corrected Akaike information criterion, was used. Speciﬁcally, the importance of each variable as the sum of the Akaike weights was calculated using the GLMULTI package, and a cutoff of 0.8 was set to distinguish between the important and unimportant variables (Calcagno & Mazancourt, 2010), as in several previous studies (Cheng et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2022). In order to verify the robustness of the results, a multivariate linear mixed model and hierarchical partitioning analysis were also used to assess the importance of factors to predict plant N uptake preference (Jin et al., 2024; Teng et al., 2024). To quantify the direct and indirect effects of multiple driving variables on plant N preferences, a structural equation model (SEM) was then used. This approach can partition the direct and indirect effects that one variable may have on another and is therefore useful for exploring complex relationships in natural ecosystems (Grace, 2006; Chen et al., 2019). SEM testing was performed using the PIECEWISESEM and LME4 packages in R. Directional-separation tests were applied to check for any missing signiﬁcant paths and for unnecessary insigniﬁcant paths that needed to be excluded.

These results suggest that further studies on different plant functional groups across broad climatic regions are warranted to further verify the climatic patterns observed in the current study. It has been suggested that compared with low-latitude ecosystems, plants in high-latitude ecosystems rely more on soil dissolved organic N, where much of the N pool is bound to organic matter and must be depolymerized by soil microorganisms whose activity is limited by low temperatures (N€asholm et al., 2009; Britto & Kronzucker, 2013; Hu et al., 2024). In partial support of this hypothesis, we found that compared with other climatic regions, the preference for glycine was lowest in (sub)tropical regions (Fig. 2), which typically have abundant soil inorganic N sources (Du et al., 2020; Mason et al., 2022). However, there were insigniﬁcant differences in organic N preference between subtropical and boreal or arctic regions. Similarly, no signiﬁcant changes in organic N uptake were also observed among biomes or plant functional types. The reason for the patterns of plant organic absorption may be partly due to the effect of soil water content. Soil moisture can signiﬁcantly change plant glycine N absorption by affecting glycine diffusion and migration from the soil to plant roots (McMurtrie & N€asholm, 2018; Liang et al., 2022). In the current study, we found that among multiple environmental factors, soil water content was the most important determinant of plant preference for organic N uptake (Figs 4, S5a). However, there were no signiﬁcant differences in soil water content among biomes or plant functional types (Fig. S5b,c), which may result in insigniﬁcant changes in organic N uptake among biomes or plant functional types. It is worth noting that the signiﬁcance and explanatory power of the current environmental variables for organic N are low (Fig. 4). This suggests that there are other factors (e.g. soil microbial competition, plant physiology, and mycorrhizal symbiosis) (N€asholm et al., 2009; T€unnermann et al., 2025) that regulate the patterns of organic N uptake. Unfortunately, these factors could not be included in the current analysis due to a lack of data in the literature.

This ﬁnding suggests that we cannot judge the utilization ability and fractional contribution of a given N resource to plants based on soil N availability alone. A number of recent studies have revealed signiﬁcant spatial variability in the shifts in N deposition composition (i.e. NHx/NOy) (Li et al., 2016; Yu et al., 2019), which may lead to changes in soil N form availability and distinct fates of plants with different N preferences and associated ecosystem functions, particularly plant C sinks. Soil water availability is also a crucial factor driving plant N uptake due to nitrogen–water interactions (Wang et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2022). It has been noted that plants prefer NO3 uptake under dry soil conditions, whereas plants prefer NH4 uptake in wetter soil environments (Houlton et al., 2007; Wang & Macko, 2011).

First, the uneven distribution of study sites across different climate zones in the current study may lead to biases in the average plant N preference (e.g. overestimation of glycine N uptake preference due to signiﬁcantly more data in alpine and temperate regions with greater organic N preference than that in subtropical regions) on a global scale (Persson & N€asholm, 2008). In addition, the pattern of plant preference for organic N uptake in our study was based on glycine. Recent studies have suggested that plants can take up different organic N forms besides amino acids (Liu et al., 2017; Moreau et al., 2019). Therefore, the conclusions drawn from a simple glycine model may not fully reﬂect the potential organic N uptake by plants (Warren, 2013). To accurately assess the ecological signiﬁcance and importance of organic N as a plant N resource, further experiments using multiple organic N forms labelled with 13C–15N in broader climatic regions are recommended.

text: Additionally, it is unclear whether plant N preference strategies and the factors regulating such strategies are consistent between the species and ecosystem levels. More ﬁeld observations of N preference at community and ecosystem scales are needed to further extend our ﬁndings. Second, although we have done our best to include factors to clarify the drivers inﬂuencing the variations of plant N uptake preference, a signiﬁcant proportion of the variability in plant N preference remains unexplained, in part due to the limited data on soil microorganisms. Soil microorganisms strongly control plant N uptake (Hill & Jones, 2019). In the short term, microbes are more efﬁcient than plants at inorganic and organic N uptake (Harrison et al., 2008). This may be due to the rapid growth rates and high surface-area-to-volume ratios of microorganisms compared with plant roots in different ecosystems (Kuzyakov & Xu, 2013). Experiments have shown that plants can compete with soil + (Mckane microbes for amino acids as well as for NH4 et al., 2002), contrary to the previous speculation. In this study, soil microbial biomass N showed insigniﬁcant correlations with plant N uptake preference (Fig. S6), which may be partly due to limited data (less than one ﬁfth of the studies included information on microbial biomass). To fully understand how plants take up N, it is important to understand how N interacts with microorganisms. Therefore, further studies using 15N tracers are needed to compare how plants take up N and how microorganisms immobilize it at the same time. Furthermore, although we have considered the role of plant functional types on plant N preference, the role of phylogeny in driving plant N preference is still an open question. To better understand plant N preference strategy and underlying mechanisms under environmental change, further investigation of plant N preference responses in a phylogenetic context is needed.
